mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI or 350 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement OM642 engine for a C320 CDI or C350 CDI typically costs between £600 and £5,200 depending on condition. Used units start from £600-£2,200, reconditioned from £1,800-£4,400, and fully rebuilt from £2,200-£5,200. Labour for supply & fit adds £500-£1,000.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common problem with the OM642 V6 diesel in the C-Class?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common problem is oil cooler seal failure, typically occurring at 70,000-120,000 miles. The seals degrade over time, causing oil to leak from the Vee of the engine. Symptoms include a 'Check Oil Level' message, decreasing oil levels, and oil stains or puddles underneath the vehicle. Mercedes Service Bulletin LI18.30-P-055434 addresses this issue. Repair costs at a specialist are approximately £800-£1,200.

mainEntity.name: Does the C-Class 320 CDI or 350 CDI have a timing belt or timing chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both the C320 CDI and C350 CDI use the OM642 V6 diesel engine, which has a timing chain, not a belt. The OM642 features a duplex roller chain per cylinder bank. Neither has a scheduled replacement interval, but tensioner wear can occur at higher mileages. A rattling noise on cold start may indicate timing chain tensioner wear.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI or 350 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the generation and condition. A W203 C320 CDI is typically worth £2,000-£5,000 - a full engine replacement often exceeds the car's value, making a used engine or targeted repair more economical. A W204 C350 CDI is worth £4,000-£10,000 - a rebuilt OM642 engine (£2,800-£5,200) can be a worthwhile investment if the car is in good condition.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the C320 CDI and C350 CDI engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both use the OM642 3.0-litre V6 diesel architecture, but with different power outputs. The C320 CDI (W203, 2004-2007) produces 221 hp (165 kW) and 510 Nm torque. The C320 CDI (W204, 2007-2011) produces 224 hp (165 kW). The C350 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY (2011-2014) produces 231 hp (170 kW) and 540 Nm torque. The later C350 CDI 4MATIC produces 265 hp (195 kW) in some markets.

mainEntity.name: What causes the Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI / 350 CDI to lose power?

acceptedAnswer.text: Power loss in the C320 CDI and C350 CDI is most commonly caused by turbocharger issues (sticking variable vanes), EGR valve clogging, or swirl flap motor failure. The swirl flap motor failure can trigger fault codes and reduce power, with repair costs at a specialist quoted at approximately £2,000-£3,000. A diagnostic check with Mercedes STAR or compatible equipment is essential to identify the exact cause.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI / 350 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The C320 CDI and C350 CDI badges represent the flagship V6 diesel offerings across two generations of the Mercedes-Benz C-Class. The C320 CDI arrived with the W203 generation in 2004, powered by Mercedes' first V6 diesel - the OM642. The C350 CDI succeeded it in the W204 generation, offering increased power and refinement. Both engines share the same 3.0-litre V6 architecture, but the C350 CDI received significant updates including higher output and BlueEFFICIENCY technology.

milestones.description: OM642.910, 3.0L V6 diesel, 221 hp (165 kW) - W203 C320 CDI launch; 510 Nm torque; 0-62 mph in 7.4 seconds; 7G-TRONIC automatic
OM642.960, 3.0L V6 diesel, 224 hp (165 kW) - W204 C320 CDI launch; 510 Nm torque
OM642.961, 3.0L V6 diesel, 224 hp - W204 C320 CDI 4MATIC variant
C320 CDI rebadged as C350 CDI; OM642.960 continues with revised calibration
OM642.834, 3.0L V6 diesel, 231 hp (170 kW) - W204 C350 CDI BlueEFFICIENCY launch; 540 Nm torque; Euro 5 emissions
W204 production ends; C350 CDI badge discontinued

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every engine fitted to the Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI and 350 CDI is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI / 350 CDI Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The C320 CDI and C350 CDI are powered by Mercedes' OM642 3.0-litre V6 diesel - a smooth, powerful engine that delivers effortless torque. However, the OM642 has well-documented weak points that can lead to expensive repairs. The oil cooler seal leak is the most common failure, followed by swirl flap motor failure and turbocharger issues. Rebuilt C320 CDI and C350 CDI engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components designed to address the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: OM642 Oil Cooler Seal Leak - The #1 V6 Diesel Failure in the C320 / C350 CDI
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI and 350 CDI (all OM642 variants, W203 and W204, 2004-2014)
problems.rootCause: The oil cooler seals, located deep within the Vee of the engine, degrade over time due to heat exposure. This causes oil to leak from the engine Vee, often visible as oil stains on the driveway or a "Check Oil Level" message. Mercedes Service Bulletin LI18.30-P-055434 addresses this issue. The seals themselves are a £10-£20 part, but the labour to access them is extensive.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of oil cooler seals, intake manifold removal, oil flush, replacement of oil-soaked wiring loom sections
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught early; prevents oil starvation damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Oil cooler seals plus turbocharger inspection, oil feed line cleaning, full oil system flush
repairOptions.longevity: Required if oil level has dropped significantly

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new oil cooler seals, upgraded loom, and rebuilt turbocharger
repairOptions.longevity: Required if oil starvation has caused bearing or turbo damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W204 C350 CDI is worth £4,000-£10,000, while a W203 C320 CDI is worth £2,000-£5,000. For W203 vehicles, a full engine replacement often exceeds the car's value - a targeted oil cooler seal repair (£800-£1,200) is usually the better financial decision. For W204 vehicles in good condition, a rebuilt OM642 with warranty (£2,800-£5,200) can be a worthwhile investment.
problems.recommendation: The OM642 oil cooler leak is a well-documented and predictable failure. Check your C320 CDI or C350 CDI's driveway for oil spots and inspect the loom near the ECU for oil wicking. Catch it early, and an £800-£1,200 specialist seal replacement is straightforward. On a C Class worth £4,000-£10,000, if the engine has already suffered oil starvation damage, replacement is the only safe route.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt OM642 Mercedes-Benz C320 CDI / C350 CDI engine prices

problems.h4: OM642 Swirl Flap Motor Failure - Intake Manifold Issues in the C320 / C350 CDI
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI and 350 CDI (OM642.960 and later variants, W204, 2007-2014)
problems.rootCause: The intake port shutoff motor (swirl flap motor) controls flaps in the intake manifold to optimise airflow. Carbon buildup can cause the flaps to stick or the motor to fail, triggering fault codes and reducing power. Repair costs at a specialist are quoted at approximately £2,000-£3,000 to investigate and replace the motor, gaskets and seals.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace swirl flap motor, intake manifold gaskets, and seals
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught early; prevents manifold damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace complete intake manifold with integrated swirl flaps
repairOptions.longevity: Required if flaps have broken or motor has failed

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new intake manifold and swirl flap components
repairOptions.longevity: Required if debris from failed flaps has entered the engine

problems.recommendation: If your C320 CDI or C350 CDI experiences rough running or a loss of power, have the swirl flap motor inspected. A £1,200-£1,800 specialist replacement is significantly cheaper than a full engine replacement. Regular carbon cleaning can help prevent swirl flap issues.

problems.h4: OM642 Turbocharger & EGR Valve Issues - Boost Loss and Reduced Performance
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz C-Class 320 CDI and 350 CDI (all OM642 variants, 2004-2014)
problems.rootCause: The variable geometry turbocharger can suffer from sticking vanes due to carbon buildup, causing loss of boost and reduced power. EGR valve clogging is also common, particularly on vehicles used for short journeys. Signs of turbo failure include loss of power, excessive smoke, increased oil consumption or a whining noise under load.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove and clean EGR valve; or replace if necessary
repairOptions.longevity: Viable; carbon buildup is the main cause

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace or rebuild turbocharger, oil feed lines
repairOptions.longevity: Required if turbo has failed or vanes are seized

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new turbo and EGR components
repairOptions.longevity: Only if turbo failure has caused engine damage

problems.recommendation: If your C320 CDI or C350 CDI experiences loss of power, have the turbocharger and EGR system inspected. A £300-£600 EGR clean or £1,200-£2,000 turbo repair is significantly cheaper than a full engine replacement. Regular motorway driving helps keep the EGR and turbo vanes clear.
